title: Introduce cache failure
description: Project: Introduce cache failure. Build and understand this project with step-by-step guidance.

data.text: Caching is one of the most effective performance optimizations available, but it introduces failure modes that do not exist without it. A cache failure can mean slow responses, stale data, or a cascading database outage. This lesson covers cache failure patterns, invalidation strategies, and how to build a cache layer that degrades gracefully under failure.

items: Cache stampede: a popular key expires and all requests hit the database simultaneously
Thundering herd: multiple concurrent requests recompute the same expensive value
Cache penetration: queries for data that never exists bypass the cache and hit the database every time
Cache avalanche: many keys expire at the same time, causing a sudden load spike
Stale data serving after an invalidation failure, leading to user-visible inconsistencies
Redis failover without proper sentinel or cluster configuration causing connection drops

terms.definition: The application reads from the cache and falls back to the database on a miss, then writes the result back to the cache.
Time-to-live: the duration after which a cached entry expires and is removed or marked stale.
A sudden surge of requests for an expired key that all try to recompute or fetch the value simultaneously.
A small random delay added to TTLs or retries to prevent synchronized behavior across clients.
A cache strategy where writes go to both the cache and the data store simultaneously, keeping them consistent.

data.text: The safest cache architecture treats the cache as optional. Every cache read should have a fast fallback to the database, and every cache write should be retried idempotently. If you find yourself building logic that is too complex to run without the cache, the cache has become a single point of failure rather than an optimization.

data.title: Cache-aside with jittered TTL
data.content: A Redis-backed cache wrapper that adds jitter to prevent stampedes:

items: Use cache keys that include a version or timestamp prefix for bulk invalidation
Delete related keys explicitly on writes instead of relying solely on TTL
Use Redis key notifications or Pub/Sub to trigger proactive invalidation across instances
Keep critical reads consistent by querying the database when a transaction commits
Monitor cache hit rate and p95 latency separately to detect degradation early

cards.title: Cache-aside (lazy loading)
cards.description: Application handles cache misses by loading from the database on demand.

cards.title: Write-through
cards.description: Writes update both cache and database synchronously.

cards.title: Write-behind (write-back)
cards.description: Writes update cache immediately and flush to the database asynchronously.
cons: Risk of data loss on crash

data.title: Monitor cache hit rate, not just latency
data.text: A cache that serves all requests from memory is fast, but a cache that misses on every request is just an expensive database proxy. Alert on hit rate drops below 80 percent before latency increases.

items.question: What should the Redis eviction policy be?
items.answer: Use allkeys-lru for caches where any key can be recomputed. Use volatile-lru if you need TTL-based eviction for specific keys. Avoid noeviction unless you have a clear memory limit and monitoring; it causes write failures when memory is full.

items.question: How do I handle a Redis outage?
items.answer: Route requests directly to the database, but ensure the database can handle the load. Use connection timeouts on the Redis client so the fallback triggers within milliseconds, not seconds.

items.question: Should I cache database query results or domain objects?
items.answer: Cache query results if the data is read-heavy and changes infrequently. Cache domain objects if they are expensive to serialize or assemble. The choice affects invalidation complexity more than performance.

data.title: Harden an existing cache layer
data.description: Your application uses Redis without jittered TTLs, without fallback on Redis failure, and without monitoring. Enhance the cache wrapper to handle these gaps.
steps: Add jitter to all TTL assignments to reduce stampede risk
Configure Redis connection timeout and retry policy
Add a cache hit rate metric and an alert threshold
Implement a fallback path when Redis is unreachable
data.expectedOutcome: You should have a cache wrapper that survives Redis failures, prevents synchronized expiry, and reports its own health metrics.

data.title: Summary
points: Treat the cache as optional; every cache read needs a database fallback
Add jitter to TTLs to prevent synchronized cache stampedes
Use database unique constraints as the final guard against duplicate writes
Monitor hit rate and alert before latency degrades
Choose an invalidation strategy that matches your consistency requirements
data.takeaway: Caching is a reliability decision, not just a performance decision. A senior engineer designs caches that degrade gracefully and never become a hidden single point of failure.
